raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old male patient was referred to Mirriah District Hospital located at 20 km from Zinder, the regional capital, for a fever associated with vomiting and sudden onset of a consciousness disorder. A week earlier, he had received malaria rapid diagnostic tests (RDT), positive result reflecting the presence of Plasmodium falciparum antigen in the blood. This prompted the initiation of an antimalarial treatment based on quinine injection at a rate of 25 mg/kg/day, which was discontinued after 3 days. Treatment was resumed 4 days later after the reappearance of symptoms. On the third day after resumption of treatment, corresponding to 10 days after the onset of symptoms, the patient was referred to Zinder National Hospital following a clinical aggravation marked by impaired consciousness. On arrival, clinical examination revealed a fever at 39 C, impaired consciousness with a Glasgow score of 11, mucous membrane pallor, conjunctival jaundice (Figure 1(a)), tachypnea with 40 cycles/min, bronchial rales, and tachycardia at 120 beats/min.
The haemodynamic state was stable with a blood pressure of 120/80 mm Hg. Urine was Coca-Cola colored (Figure 2), which led to the diagnosis of BWF. Test strip urine examination revealed hemoglobinuria at 2 plus, bilirubinuria 3 plus, proteinuria 2 plus, and absence of urobilinogens, red blood cells, and leucocytes. The malaria RDT was positive, while the thick peripheral blood smear was negative. Biological examinations showed leucocytosis of 15000 elements/mm3, normochromic anaemia with a hemoglobin level of 4 g/dl, and a normal platelet count of 194,000/mm3. The direct Coombs test was negative. Urea: 74.9 mmol/L, serum creatinine: 559.6 mumol/L, proteinuria: 0.56 g/24 h, ASAT: 334 IU/L, ALAT: 185 IU/L, CRP: 92 mg/L, blood ionogram: 128 mEq/L of sodium and 5 mEq/L of potassium, TP: 100%, INR: 0.99, TCA: 29.5, TQ: 12 sec, and a blood bilirubin level of 200 mg/L predominantly unconjugated. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys, discrete renal dedifferentiation, and vesicular sludge. This presentation required dialysis for uremic syndrome. The patient received 3 hemodialysis sessions with transfusion of erythrocyte concentrates. The antimalarial treatment was continued with an intramuscular artemether derivative. Clinical status and renal function normalized after 7 days. The patient was discharged cured.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male was referred to Zinder National Hospital, Niger, with a 10-day history of fever, vomiting, dark 'Coca-Cola-colored' urine, and sudden-onset impaired consciousness following interrupted parenteral quinine therapy.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Diagnosed 10 days earlier with P. falciparum malaria by RDT, the patient received injectable quinine (25 mg/kg/day) for 3 days, stopped treatment, and resumed quinine 4 days later when symptoms recurred. On day 3 after resuming quinine (day 10 of illness), he developed impaired consciousness, jaundice, and Coca-Cola-colored urine.
subjective.past_medical_history: Treated with interrupted courses of injectable quinine (25 mg/kg/day) over the preceding 10 days for RDT-positive P. falciparum malaria.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, vomiting, impaired consciousness, jaundice, and dark Coca-Cola-colored urine.

objective.physical_examination: Temperature 39 C, Glasgow Coma Scale score 11, BP 120/80 mmHg, HR 120 bpm, RR 40 cycles/min, mucous membrane pallor, conjunctival jaundice, bronchial rales, and Coca-Cola-colored urine.
objective.routine_investigations: WBC 15,000/mm3, severe normochromic anemia with Hb 4 g/dL, platelets 194,000/mm3, negative direct Coombs test, urea 74.9 mmol/L, creatinine 559.6 umol/L, 24-hour proteinuria 0.56 g/24 h, AST 334 IU/L, ALT 185 IU/L, total bilirubin 200 mg/L (predominantly unconjugated), CRP 92 mg/L, Na 128 mEq/L, K 5 mEq/L, PT 100%, INR 0.99, aPTT 29.5 s, TQ 12 s. Urine dipstick showed hemoglobinuria 2+, bilirubinuria 3+, proteinuria 2+, and absent RBCs, WBCs, and urobilinogen. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal-sized kidneys with mild corticomedullary dedifferentiation and gallbladder sludge.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Quinine-triggered blackwater fever (BWF) complicated by severe acute intravascular hemolysis (Hb 4 g/dL) and uremic acute kidney injury following Plasmodium falciparum malaria. Malaria RDT was positive for P. falciparum while thick peripheral blood smear was negative on admission. Managed by discontinuing quinine, switching to intramuscular artemether derivative, transfusing packed RBCs, and performing 3 sessions of hemodialysis; clinical status and renal function normalized within 7 days and he was discharged cured.
